concepts.title: Array versus List in Python
concepts.definition: A NumPy array (officially ndarray) keeps one single data type for all its elements and lays them side by side in one continuous block of memory, which makes it compact and fast. A core-Python list may mix types, stores them scattered in memory, and cannot do element-wise arithmetic, while an array happily evaluates A1 / 3 on every element at once.
concepts.key_idea: Homogeneous type plus contiguous storage buys speed and element-wise operations that lists cannot offer.

why are operations on arrays faster than on lists

solution_steps.explain: a list may hold mixed types; every element of an array must share one dtype
array elements sit contiguously, list elements are scattered with type tags
dividing an array by 3 scales every element; the same expression fails for a mixed list

worked_examples.q: Which structure stores one single data type in one continuous memory block: a list or a NumPy array?

concepts.title: ndarray Attributes: shape, size, itemsize
concepts.definition: Every ndarray reports its structure through attributes: ndim counts the axes (the rank), shape lists the size along each axis, size totals the elements (the product of the shape numbers), dtype names the element type, and itemsize gives each element's width in bytes, obtained by dividing the type's bit width by 8.
concepts.key_idea: Multiply the shape entries for size, divide the type bits by 8 for itemsize, then multiply the two for the array's memory footprint.

solution_steps.action: convert the type width to bytes
solution_steps.explain: 8 bits form a byte, so integer-divide the type's bit count by 8
the size equals rows multiplied by columns

solution_steps.action: scale up to the whole array
solution_steps.explain: memory used is the element count times each element's byte width

concepts.title: Two Dimensional Array Indexing
concepts.definition: A 2-D array addresses each cell with a pair of zero-based indices marks[i, j], where i counts rows and j counts columns. Counting the cells stored before a given one shows why the pair works: whole rows of the grid come first, then the offset inside the row.
concepts.key_idea: Row index times row length skips whole rows; adding the column index lands on the exact cell, and an index past an axis size raises IndexError.

solution_steps.explain: each full row holds column_count cells, so the row index skips that many elements
adding the column index reaches the wanted cell in row-major storage

concepts.title: Matrix Multiplication Cell Value
concepts.definition: The @ operator multiplies two matrices properly (unlike * which pairs elements). Each cell of the answer is built by walking one row of the left matrix against one column of the right matrix: multiply the matched pairs and add the products.
concepts.key_idea: Row meets column: multiply pairwise, then add the products; element-wise * needs equal shapes but @ needs matching inner dimensions.

their sum is the cell of the product matrix

concepts.title: Statistical Operations: sum, mean, axis
concepts.definition: NumPy computes descriptive statistics straight on arrays: sum() totals the elements, mean() averages them, max() and min() fetch the extremes, std() spreads them. An axis argument chooses direction: axis=1 collapses each row into one number, axis=0 collapses each column.
concepts.key_idea: Add a row's cells for its row sum, divide by the row length for its mean; axis picks rows or columns.

solution_steps.explain: add the two cells of row one

adding the row totals gives the grand sum over axis=1 then axis=0
the overall mean divides the grand total by the element count

concepts.title: Reshape Without Losing Elements
concepts.definition: reshape() rearranges an array's elements into a new grid without adding, dropping or reordering values, so the element count must stay fixed. Choosing a new column count fixes the row count automatically by dividing the unchanged total among the columns.
concepts.key_idea: Reshape re-cuts the same elements into new rows and columns; the product of the new shape must reproduce the old size exactly.

solution_steps.action: count the elements to be rearranged

solution_steps.action: distribute them over the new columns
solution_steps.explain: integer-dividing the unchanged total by the new column count gives the required row count

concepts.title: arange Start Stop Step Values
concepts.definition: np.arange(start, stop, step) builds an array of evenly spaced values beginning at start, advancing by step, and stopping before stop. Counting its elements and its final value follows the same upward-rounded arithmetic as Python's range.
concepts.key_idea: Round the span upward against the step to count the values; the last one sits one step short of stop.

concepts.title: Concatenating Arrays Row wise and Column wise
concepts.definition: np.concatenate() joins arrays along an axis: axis=0 stacks them one beneath the other, axis=1 places them side by side. Every dimension except the joining axis must match exactly, or NumPy raises a ValueError.
concepts.key_idea: Joining side by side adds the column counts and demands equal row counts; joining downward does the reverse.

the unchanged row count times the new column count gives the total elements of the joined array

concepts.title: Splitting Arrays Into Subarrays
concepts.definition: np.split() cuts an array into pieces, either at a list of index positions or into N equal parts, along a chosen axis. Cutting a 5-row array at positions [1, 3] yields a one-row head, a two-row middle and a two-row tail, and the parts together always rebuild the original row count.
concepts.key_idea: Each cut index marks where one part ends and the next begins; subtracting successive cut points sizes every middle part.
question_patterns: array4 with 5 rows is split at row indices [1,3]; how many rows do the second and third parts hold together

solution_steps.explain: the rows between the two cut indices number cut_two minus cut_one
the rows after the final cut are the total minus cut_two
the second and third sub-arrays together hold the middle plus the tail rows

worked_examples.q: A 5-row array splits at positions [1, 3]. How many rows does the middle part hold?

concepts.title: Transpose of an Array
concepts.definition: transpose() swaps the roles of rows and columns, exactly like the transpose of a school mathematics matrix: a 3 by 4 grid comes back as 4 by 3, and the original array itself stays untouched unless the result is stored back.
concepts.key_idea: Transpose flips the shape pair; the value at row i, column j moves to row j, column i.

the cell at position (i, j) relocates to (j, i) while the original array remains unchanged
